questions.question: Why does the evaluator use a paired t test instead of comparing two single numbers?
options: Because numpy requires paired arrays
Because the runner cannot emit a single number
Because t tests are always required by IRB
Because pairing the same seed across candidate and baseline isolates the configuration change from random initialisation noise
questions.explanation: Pairing by seed cancels out random initialisation effects. The remaining difference is attributable to the configuration change, which is what the test measures.

questions.question: Why does the evaluator carry a direction field on every metric?
options: Because accuracy and loss point in opposite ways; the sign of the improvement depends on which direction is better for the metric being compared
Because the runner requires it
Because numpy needs the direction for variance
Because the parser expects it
questions.explanation: Higher is better metrics improve when they go up; lower is better metrics improve when they go down. The direction field tells the improvement function which sign convention to apply.

questions.question: What does the verdict path return when |improvement| is below the threshold even if the p value is significant?
options: improved
noise
regressed
failed
questions.explanation: A statistically significant change that is too small to act on is still noise from the loop's point of view. The threshold gate runs before the significance gate.

questions.question: Why does the evaluator transform log scaled metrics before computing improvement?
options: Because numpy logs are faster
Because the p value depends on it
Because perplexity and similar metrics grow exponentially with loss; transforming to log space makes a threshold like two percent meaningful across linear and log metrics
Because the runner only emits log scaled metrics
questions.explanation: Perplexity is exp(loss). A small loss change is a large perplexity change. Taking the log keeps relative improvements comparable to linear metrics under one threshold.

questions.question: When does paired_t_test return p_value=None?
options: Whenever the metric is log-scaled, because logarithms cannot be tested.
Whenever the paired differences have zero variance, because the helper cannot represent a t statistic.
When fewer than two paired samples are available; with zero variance and at least two samples it returns 1.0 for a zero mean difference or 0.0 otherwise.
Whenever candidate and baseline means are equal, because a zero effect has no p-value.
questions.explanation: The code returns None only for n < 2. For constant paired differences with n >= 2, it handles the zero-variance case explicitly instead of returning None.

questions.question: What happens if even one candidate result has a terminal label other than ok?
options: The evaluator returns a failed verdict and records the bad terminals in the rationale
The evaluator drops that seed and proceeds
The evaluator retries the run
The evaluator falls back to a one sided test
questions.explanation: A failed run invalidates the candidate set. The evaluator short circuits the verdict path and returns failed with the offending terminals listed, so the orchestrator does not draw a conclusion from a crashed run.
